newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-HOLYFIELD FORCED TO TAKE RIGOROUS EXAM TO FIGHT TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HOLYFIELD FORCED TO TAKE RIGOROUS EXAM TO FIGHT TYSON.

text.p: Nevada officials, wary of Evander Holyfield's past physical problems, forced him to undergo one of its most extensive examinations ever before issuing the former heavyweight champion a license to fight.

In addition to a physical examination by the famous Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, Nevada State Athletic Commission Executive Director Marc Ratner said Wednesday the commission insisted Holyfield be examined twice in the weeks leading to Saturday's fight for Mike Tyson's World Boxing Association heavyweight title.

The first public sign of physical problems for Holyfield, who ironically has a reputation as one of the world's most finely-conditioned athletes, came after he lost his world heavyweight titles to Michael Moorer in April, 1994.

Shortly after looking lethargic while losing the 12-round decision, Holyfield was diagnosed with a hole in his heart, and he retired. But after visiting a faith healer who pronounced him healthy, and then passing an examination at the Mayo Clinic, he came back to fight Ray Mercer in May, 1995.
Holyfield beat Mercer with a unanimous decision and went on to fight Riddick Bowe for a third time.
Bowe had defeated Holyfield in November, 1992 to win the world heavyweight title. Holyfield came back the next year to take back his crown.

In their rubber match, Holyfield knocked down Bowe in the sixth round for the first time in his career. Bowe staggered to his feet and seemed ready to be knocked out by anything resembling a punch. Amazingly, Holyfield, who appeared to be having trouble just raising his arms, merely stood in front of Bowe, allowing him to recover.
Bowe came back and knocked down Holyfield twice in the eighth round, and the fight was stopped shortly afterward.

Holyfield's inability to finish off Bowe, and what appeared to be difficulty breathing in his fifth-round stoppage last May of a struggling Bobby Czyz, brought more questions about the fighter's health.

Holyfield later said he had been weakened by the flu he contracted while training for the Bowe fight and was afraid to expend too much energy trying to finish Bowe for fear he would not have anything left if Bowe had survived.

"We were concerned because he looked so tired," Ratner said. "We accepted his virus (explanation) but because of this we sent doctors in at about four weeks before the fight and then two weeks before. It was the first time we ever did that.
"This time we want to know more about the training," Ratner said. "We don't want anybody saying they were hurt."

Ratner was reminded that shortly before Muhammad Ali fought Larry Holmes in 1980, Nevada officials said Ali had passed a physical examination by the Mayo Clinic, but the Nevada Commission refused to release the Mayo report.

Years later it was revealed the report said Ali had several physical problems, including difficulty with the finger-to-nose test and a hole in a membrane in his brain that could become enlarged by blows to the head, according to Tom Hauser, Ali's biographer.
"That was a different Commission," Ratner said.

He added that recently the Commission's medical advisor, Dr Charles Ruggeroli, told him after reviewing Holyfield's most recent Mayo examination, "'If we turn down Evander Holyfield for a license we can never license anybody. He had the most complete test in sports, not just boxing.'"

In a recent television promotion for Tyson-Holyfield, Ruggeroli said Holyfield "has an absolutely normal heart, and the one thing I guarantee you is that regardless of what happens in the fight his heart will not play a role in the outcome."
